title: How a Reading Works

spine.markdown: Intertext is designed to support multiple texts. For the prototype we have adapted a text previously published in print, The Digital Plenitude (Bolter 2019).

The scrollable text is located in the left pane, while the right panes present an expandable table of contents and a space for the reader to type questions or comments. The text is presented in assimilable units of about 250 words each. The reader is invited to respond, after which the system responds with another unit tailored specifically to reader’s questions or comments. The reader may choose to respond again or to continue to the next section or to any other section or chapter.

Unlike most of the current reading systems, Intertext is envisioned for new texts or texts specifically adapted by their author for digital redefinition. Each Intertext begins from a base text, which is divided into sections and summarized to constitute the spine of the interactive version. In responding to a reader, the model draws first on the spine to guide its response. It may also draw on a fund of extra interpretive or factual units as well as a list of verified citations and a set of illustrative images and videos. The model can also search the web for further information.

Intertext’s responses are generated by prompting Claude Sonnet 5.5. Each prompt is a bundle consisting of summaries of the argument and previous reader responses together with fixed rules for responding. Claude’s initial completion is then revised for style before being delivered to the reader. The two passes are designed:

- To ensure that the responses do not exhibit random drift from the base argument.
- To maintain the tone as close as possible to the author’s text and limit stylistic tics of LLMs.
- To regulate the citation of outside works from a verified library of references.

fundEntries.title: Three ways to enter
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks how a reading begins, what contributing means, or whether the original can still be read.
fundEntries.markdown: Before reading begins, the reader chooses one of three paths. To contribute is to read the evolving edition and to allow the conversation to inform later versions of the text. To read the current text is to read the same edition without saving anything. To read the original is to read the text as the author first wrote it, without any reader's changes. The choice is made once, and there is no view that compares the editions during a reading.

fundEntries.title: The boxed opening and the Return key
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks what the boxed passage is, what pressing Return does, or how a section ends.
fundEntries.markdown: Each section opens with a short boxed passage written for the reader, which sets a scene and states the section's thesis in brief. The reader may then type a question or comment, which receives an answer, or simply press Return, which carries the reading forward with the next ideas the text holds. The first Return treats the box as a prologue and begins with the first passage; later ones resume where the conversation has reached. When the section's material is exhausted, the text says so, and a further Return moves on to the next section.

fundEntries.title: Moving between sections
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks whether they can skip around, or how the text remembers what was said earlier.
fundEntries.markdown: The table of contents remains on screen, and the reader may move to any section at any time. Each section keeps its own conversation. The system also keeps a short private summary of each section the reader has visited, so that a long reading retains its continuity without the whole transcript being sent again with every turn.

fundEntries.title: The look of the page
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks about the design of the reading page or why it looks like a book.
fundEntries.markdown: The reader's page is designed as an annotated book. The reading is set as a printed page in a Garamond typeface, with labels in red small capitals and a drop cap at the start of each section. The reader's own words appear in the margin beside the reply they prompted, in italic and joined to it by a fine line, much as a reader's notes stand beside a printed text. On narrow screens they appear above the reply instead. The contents and the space for typing sit in a dark column on the right.

fundEntries.title: What the spine is
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks what the spine contains, or whether the reader ever sees the author's text itself.
fundEntries.markdown: The spine is the author's own text for each section, divided into passages. It is the authoritative route through the section, but the reader never sees it as such. When the reader presses Return, the system retells the next passages in order, closely and often in the author's own phrasing, though compressed and joined to what the conversation has already covered. When the reader asks a question, the system draws on whatever in the spine bears on it and answers in new words.

fundEntries.title: Why each section also has a statement of its argument
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks why the text needs summaries of the argument when it already holds the full text, or what keeps replies on course.
fundEntries.markdown: Besides the spine, each section and each chapter carries a short statement of its argument, written or approved by the author and never shown to the reader. The full text supplies the material; the statement supplies the direction. A section gives a passing example and its central claim roughly equal weight, and a model answering a question about a detail tends to follow the detail. The statement tells the model what is central. It guides every reply, and it is stated only when the reader's question bears on it, in fresh words and as a claim.

fundEntries.title: Why a spine and a fund
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks why the material is split into a spine and a fund, or why readers' additions do not simply go into the text.
fundEntries.markdown: A section is not a single text that is rewritten and enlarged with each reading. Additions written by a model can be intelligent and supportive and still damage the balance and rhythm of a continuous essay, because a model tends to apply an argument to more cases and to add more qualifications, whether or not they belong in the main movement. The system therefore keeps the concise route through the section, the spine, apart from optional material, the fund, which the text may draw on for a particular reader at a particular moment.

fundEntries.title: What the fund holds
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks what goes into the fund or how the text decides to use it.
fundEntries.markdown: The fund holds six kinds of material: clarifications, examples, qualifications, counterarguments, evidence and extensions. Each unit is attached to the passage it belongs with and carries a short note on when it is useful. The fund is not a checklist. The text draws on it only where it helps answer the reader's question without disturbing the movement of the section, and often it is right to leave the fund unused. Only units that have been accepted ever reach readers.

fundEntries.title: How citations are controlled
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks how the text decides what it may cite, or how hallucinated references are prevented.
fundEntries.markdown: For each section the text may cite only the works on that section's list of verified references, each described with what it says and, where known, its pages. When the text draws on one of these works, the citation is checked against the list, and anything not on it is dropped, so that an invented source cannot reach the reader. Each citation that survives appears as a numbered note with a full reference. The list also records how each writer is to be mentioned: introduced and then named, cited by note only, or, in the case of the author's own work, stated as the work's own thinking.

fundEntries.title: Images and videos
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks how the text shows images or videos, or whether it can show one.
fundEntries.markdown: A reply may show one item from the section's list of images, videos and web pages. These are checked in advance: a video is played only if it can be embedded, an image is shown only if its licence allows, with its credit beneath, and anything else appears as a card that opens in a new tab. Each item on the list carries a note on when it is worth showing, and the list is maintained by a script that checks every item rather than from memory.

fundEntries.title: Searching the web
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks whether the text knows about recent events or can look things up.
fundEntries.markdown: The model can also search the web, a few times in a single turn, for what the text does not hold: recent events, recent work, or an outside source the reader asks about. The names, dates and details in the author's text remain authoritative, and nothing found outside alters them. Whatever the model draws from a search reaches the reader as a numbered note, so that the reply itself carries no list of links.

fundEntries.title: What the model is given
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks what goes into the prompt, or how much of the text the model sees at once.
fundEntries.markdown: Each reply begins as a call to the model whose prompt puts first what stays the same throughout a section: the rules for the voice, the rule for citations, the name of the section, the statement of its argument, the opening box, the author's text for the section and its list of references. These parts are reused from turn to turn. After them comes what changes: instructions for a Return, the images not yet shown, the writers already introduced, brief summaries of other sections the reader has visited, and the units of the fund that are on offer. The conversation so far follows.

fundEntries.title: What the revision does
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks what the second pass changes, or why a reply needs revising at all.
fundEntries.markdown: The second pass receives the draft together with the statement of the argument, everything the reader has seen so far, the author's text for the section and the reader's words. It revises the reply so that it answers the question in its opening paragraph, introduces anything the reader has not yet met, keeps each claim at the strength its evidence allows, removes praise of the reader and repetition of earlier replies, and stays within 250 words. It may add no new ideas, and every citation must survive it unchanged; otherwise the draft is used instead.

fundEntries.title: A single voice
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks who is speaking, whether a passage came from the author, a reader or the model, or how the text handles an objection.
fundEntries.markdown: The text speaks as the work, in the third person and in the register of a serious discussion between equals. It does not say whether a sentence came from the author's text, a unit of the fund, an earlier reader or the model. It answers the reader's question first and then widens the answer; it meets an objection as an essay does, granting plainly what the reader has right and narrowing a claim that went too far; and it acknowledges a real factual error without fuss. The reader is assumed to know only what has appeared in the conversation.

fundEntries.title: Which models do the work
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks which models InterText uses, or how the parts of a reply are kept private.
fundEntries.markdown: Replies, revisions and the evolution of the text are all produced by Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5.5. Along with each reply the model also reports, privately, which units of the fund it used, whether the section is complete, and a short memory of the section so far. The system reads these reports and removes them before the reply is revised, its citations checked, and the result delivered to the reader.
